name: Deva

attributes.attribute: Roman variation of the word for goddess
seen as a feminine divine force
demanded human victims at regular intervals

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Deva is a British goddess. Her name means 'the goddess.' The name was borne by the British River Dee. Rivers in Celtic lands acted as a feminine divine force. The River Dee was such a force. The river was believed to demand human victims. The victims were needed at regular intervals. A folk rhyme records the demand. The rhyme runs 'Bloodthirsty Dee, each year needs three; but bonny Don, she needs none.' The Romans gave the Dee a related name. They used a variation of their own word for goddess. That word was Deva. The Roman fort at Chester carried the name Caer Deva. The goddess Deva thus named both a river and a city on its banks. The deity tied a sacred river to a Roman settlement. She connected the natural world to the imperial world. Her name carried across both domains.

okr.objective: Present Deva as the British river goddess behind the River Dee and the city of Chester.
